nameStory: The Short-eared Owl gets its name from the tiny feather tufts on its head that look like little ears - but they're so small you can barely see them! Unlike its cousin the Long-eared Owl with its prominent 'horns,' this owl's 'ears' are just stubby little tufts that only pop up when the bird feels threatened and strikes a defensive pose.
description: The Short-eared Owl is a medium-sized owl that hunts during the day over open grasslands and fields. It has a streaky brown and buff appearance that helps it blend into dried grasses, with distinctive white patches on its wings that flash when it flies. These owls are about the size of a crow, with long wings perfect for their low, swooping flight style as they patrol meadows looking for mice and voles.

idTips.label: Daylight hunter
idTips.description: Active during daylight hours, especially at dawn and dusk, flying low over fields with a distinctive moth-like, wavering flight pattern

idTips.label: Wing patches
idTips.description: Bright white patches near the wingtips and a dark 'wrist' mark on the underwing create a striking contrast visible even from a distance

idTips.label: Facial disc
idTips.description: Round facial disc with dark rings around bright yellow eyes, giving it an alert, wide-eyed expression

idTips.label: Ground behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perching on low posts, fence stakes, or directly on the ground rather than in trees

idTips.label: Streaky plumage
idTips.description: Heavily streaked brown and buff coloring that looks like dried grass, with a lighter belly marked by dark streaks

habitat: Look for Short-eared Owls in wide-open spaces like coastal grasslands, salt marshes, agricultural fields, and airports in New England. They prefer areas with low vegetation where they can hunt for small mammals, often near wetlands or prairies. These owls need large territories of open country and are most often spotted along the coast or in river valleys.

seasonality.spring: Some individuals begin returning to breeding territories, though they're uncommon nesters in New England. Watch for increased activity and territorial displays.
seasonality.summer: Rare during summer months in New England as most head north to breed. Any sightings are noteworthy and should be reported to local birding groups.
seasonality.fall: Migration brings the best viewing opportunities as northern birds move south. Peak sightings occur from October through November.
seasonality.winter: Most reliable season for spotting them as northern populations winter in New England's coastal areas and remain active during daylight hours.

funFact: Short-eared Owls are one of the most widespread birds in the world, found on every continent except Antarctica and Australia - they're essentially the cosmopolitan jet-setters of the owl world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Northern Harrier hawks, which also hunt low over grasslands during the day. Remember: owls have round faces and yellow eyes, while harriers have white rump patches and smaller heads. If you see the distinctive white wing patches and that round, flat face, you've got an owl!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'eared owls,' the ear tufts on Short-eared Owls have nothing to do with hearing - they're just feathers used for communication and camouflage. Their actual ears are hidden asymmetrically on the sides of their heads to help pinpoint prey sounds in tall grass.
compareHints: Short-eared Owls differ from Long-eared Owls by their habitat preferences and ear tufts - Long-eared Owls have prominent 'horns' and prefer wooded areas, while Short-eared Owls have barely visible tufts and stick to open grasslands. Short-eared Owls are also day-active hunters, while Long-eared Owls are strictly nocturnal and much more secretive.
